question: Why do the cybersickness-reduction techniques that restrict the field of view work on the edges of the view rather than the centre?
gold_answer: Peripheral vision is better than central vision at detecting movement (lecture 27). Vection, the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli and correlates positively with visual motion stimulus, so visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cybersickness (lecture 11). Restricting the field of view therefore reduces peripheral optical flow and ideally reduces cybersickness; an asymmetric mask obscures only peripheral regions with higher optical flow during locomotion and leaves low-flow regions visible (lecture 12). The cost is that field-of-view restriction can reduce presence and impair visual tasks (lecture 12).

question: Why did the Majuli VR tour move users between places with teleportation and a vehicle instead of letting them walk everywhere?
gold_answer: Free walking is the most natural travel technique but completely free walking is not practical; full-gait walking is confined to the physical space and mapped to a potentially infinite virtual space, with a mismatch (lecture 40). Teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic walking, and teleportation instead of steering is a listed locomotion modification for cybersickness (lectures 11, 12). In the Majuli design the island's geographic spread is large and content rich, so exploring it by walking takes a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness; a virtual vehicle metaphor (a pre-planned route, the user selects a destination) was added for long-distance travel, with controlled joystick navigation without abrupt movements, while the vehicle's viewpoint speed must be chosen carefully (lecture 41). Teleportation gives the shortest exposure but is not natural (lecture 51), so the tour combines walking within each information point with teleportation or the vehicle between points because one technique alone would not suit the large spread (lecture 59).

question: How does the finding that longer VR exposure makes people sicker turn into a method for planning a tour route?
gold_answer: Prolonged exposure through HMDs leads to greater cybersickness (lecture 11), and users are advised to avoid long continuous exposure, with roughly 55 to 70 minutes suggested as generally safe (lecture 12). The optimisation lectures therefore try to control exposure duration, which depends on world size, travelling speed, travel time and interaction time (lecture 51). The first approach represents the tour as a graph of points of interest and finds the path covering all of them in minimum time with a travelling salesman formulation using a natural walking-speed model (lecture 51). If that minimum still exceeds the time threshold above which cybersickness may occur (walking a whole satra could take up to a day), a second approach assigns each point an importance and waiting time and finds the most important path within the threshold with a vehicle-routing-with-profit solver (lectures 52, 53).

question: Which headsets, development tools and computers did the Majuli VR tour use, and how did the limits of those devices shape the app?
gold_answer: The tour was built in Unity (version 2021.3.22f1) for the Oculus Quest 2 and for Android smartphones (Android 6), using the XR toolkit for the Quest version and the Google VR SDK for the Cardboard version (lecture 44); Unity is a cross-platform engine supporting over 20 platforms (lecture 60). The evaluation used a Meta Quest 2 (1920 by 1832 pixels per eye) connected to a Windows 11 PC with a GTX 1080 GPU via Oculus Link, with joystick-based controllers (lecture 47). The Quest 2 is a standalone device with its own processor and memory but less computing power and storage than a high-end graphics workstation, so all videos were stored in the cloud, giving a 5.1 GB app that needs high bandwidth, network coverage and low latency (lectures 44, 59). For smartphones in Cardboard, images were compressed and most videos removed, cutting the size from about 10 GB to 0.7 GB at the cost of realism (lectures 44, 59).

question: What different ways can an XR system track the user, and what are the strengths and weaknesses of each?
gold_answer: Head tracking is the most important thing to track in VR (lecture 13); full-body tracking can use several surrounding cameras that see reflective markers on a suit (lecture 14). By sensor position, outside-in tracking uses external sensors or markers and is restricted to the area where they are placed, whereas inside-out tracking carries the sensors with the user and works anywhere (lecture 16). Inertial tracking in an IMU relies mainly on the gyroscope, which drifts, so drift correction needs at least two sensors blended, for example a gyroscope with a camera, accelerometer or magnetometer using a gain parameter alpha (lecture 17). Other tracker families are electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic, vision-based (infrared tracking is unaffected by poor lighting and shadows), inertial and hybrid; SLAM gives drift-free tracking of unknown environments, and GPS tracks position outdoors but is less accurate indoors (lecture 18).

question: What can developers, designers and users do to reduce cybersickness, from the headset to the design of a whole tour?
gold_answer: Developer-side strategies are field-of-view adjustment (which reduces peripheral optical flow but can reduce presence), dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations such as phantom legs, floor vibrations and modified motion platforms, and locomotion changes such as teleportation instead of steering; users can limit continuous exposure (about 55 to 70 minutes), habituate with repeated short exposures, use slow diaphragmatic breathing, and use pleasant music and air flow (lecture 12). The cybersickness guidelines are VR-specific design guidelines and may not apply to AR (lecture 38). The Majuli design used controlled joystick navigation without abrupt movement and a vehicle metaphor whose viewpoint speed must be chosen carefully (lecture 41). The optimisation lectures reduce exposure duration with a minimum-time path and, if that exceeds the cybersickness time threshold, a most-important-points path within the threshold (lectures 51, 52, 53).

question: What does Unity's render pipeline support build on from earlier in the course?
gold_answer: The Unity lectures aim at support for the graphics pipeline discussed earlier (object definition, scene construction, lighting, view transformation, scan conversion) so a developer need not implement it (lecture 60). The earlier pipeline has five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, viewing transformation and scan conversion (lecture 55); Unity's model files carry the object definition as meshes, the popular mesh representation of lecture 55, plus materials and textures (lecture 61). Lighting from lecture 56 is supported by Unity lights and shadows (lecture 61), and the camera set-up of the viewing stage in lecture 57 is done in Unity by adding a camera, after which Unity does the other calculations (lecture 61). Scan conversion and rendering with GPUs and graphics libraries (lecture 58) are handled by Unity through native libraries such as DirectX, Metal, OpenGL and Vulkan (lecture 61).

question: What earlier ideas does the evaluation of the Majuli VR tour rest on?
gold_answer: Presence is a psychological state of being in the virtual environment, distinct from immersion (lecture 8), and cybersickness is measured with questionnaires such as the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire with 16 items in three subscales (lecture 11; lecture 44 repeats SSQ as the most used cybersickness questionnaire). The evaluation uses the empirical-study process of research question, variables, controlled experiment (lecture 45) and experiment design with representative participants, 12 to 25 generally being enough (lecture 46). The three user categories identified in the design, pilgrims, students and tourists (lecture 41), were the groups of the 27 participants (lecture 47). It measured presence with the QEP questionnaire and cybersickness with the SSQ before and after exposure, finding good presence and a significant pre-post change only in oculomotor and total sickness (lecture 47).

question: What earlier ideas does the resource optimisation of the Majuli app for the Quest 2 and phones rest on?
gold_answer: The hardware lecture says a VR system's processing element is typically a PC or a high-end workstation with a good GPU, useful for rendering complex scenes (lecture 14). The human factors lecture says VR needs frame rates much higher than the 24 or 60 fps of television and film, and the resource lecture notes a higher refresh rate is preferable (lectures 28, 54); VR is resource hungry and the aim is a good experience on affordable hardware (lecture 54). Interactive VR redraws the scene with every input and anti-aliasing adds further computation, so rendering cost grows manifold and GPUs exploit the parallelism (lecture 58). Hence the Quest 2, with less compute and storage than a workstation and about 10 GB of rich content, needed cloud storage for videos (with bandwidth, coverage and latency demands), and phones needed compressed images, no video and in extreme cases removed features (lecture 59).

question: How are presence and cybersickness related in this course, and when does reducing one cost the other?
gold_answer: Control over motion affects presence directly and cybersickness indirectly through presence; greater presence generally leads to lower cybersickness, though not always (lecture 11). A sensory mismatch can cause cybersickness for some users, and when the user consciously notices the conflict presence is compromised (lecture 26). Mitigation is a trade-off: restricting the field of view reduces cybersickness but can reduce presence (lecture 12), so mitigation must avoid compromising presence (lecture 49). The Majuli evaluation measured both, presence with the QEP questionnaire and cybersickness with the SSQ before and after exposure, finding good presence but significant changes in oculomotor and total sickness (lecture 47).

question: How can a smartphone in a cardboard box give a 3D headset experience, and what did the Majuli tour give up in its Cardboard version?
gold_answer: In stereoscopy each eye views its own image at the same time and the brain combines the left and right images into a 3D view, aided by binocular vision (lecture 28). A cardboard housing holds a smartphone, and if the phone displays stereoscopic views, wearing it as a headset gives an immersive environment without an expensive headset; it costs only about 500 to 1000 rupees (lecture 59). The Majuli Cardboard version used Unity with the Google VR SDK on Android 6 (lecture 44). To fit phones the images were compressed and most videos removed, shrinking the app to 0.7 GB from roughly 10 GB, which made the experience less realistic than the full version (lectures 44, 59).

question: Why might adding vibration or motion cues to a VR setup reduce cybersickness?
gold_answer: Motion sickness occurs when the brain receives conflicting signals from different senses, with symptoms similar to cybersickness (lecture 10). In vection, vision reports that the user is moving or accelerating while the balance sense and proprioception say the user is motionless, and the goal should be to balance the experience across senses (lecture 26). The mitigation lecture lists hardware-level alterations that add matching cues: phantom legs (haptic cues synchronised to footsteps, reduced cybersickness to a great extent), floor vibrations matching the virtual environment, sound with vibration, and modified motion platforms where short bursts of rotational acceleration matched visual forward acceleration and were quite effective (lecture 12). The hardware lecture presents haptics and motion platforms, which move the whole body to give a sense of physical motion and gravity, as VR output devices (lecture 14).
